summary:
FIRETRACE is a satellite-based fire intelligence platform designed to analyze, visualize, and understand wildfire activity across the globe using historical and near-real-time satellite observations. It integrates fire detection data from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments, including Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, and NOAA-20 satellites.

The platform processes millions of historical fire observations to identify spatial and temporal patterns, compare detections across satellite sensors, and explore changes in fire activity over time. It provides an interactive 3D globe, geographic fire visualization, sensor-based filtering, historical timelines, and analytical summaries to help users investigate fire hotspots and understand their distribution.

FIRETRACE also explores cross-sensor observation matching using spatial and temporal proximity, alongside historical analysis and fire radiative power comparisons. Its goal is to improve the interpretation and consistency of satellite-derived fire observations while communicating uncertainty and data-quality limitations.

By combining satellite datasets, geospatial visualization, and analytical techniques, FIRETRACE aims to transform complex fire observation data into an accessible intelligence platform that can support researchers, environmental analysts, disaster management teams, and policymakers in understanding wildfire patterns and strengthening fire-monitoring capabilities.
details:
FIRETRACE – Project Description

FIRETRACE is a satellite-based global fire intelligence platform that transforms large-scale satellite fire observations into meaningful, interactive information for understanding wildfire activity. It uses NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite datasets from Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, and NOAA-20 to explore fire locations, historical trends, and differences between satellite observations.

What does it do and how does it work?

FIRETRACE collects and processes satellite fire observation datasets containing information such as latitude, longitude, acquisition date and time, fire radiative power (FRP), and sensor details. It standardizes and analyzes these observations to identify spatial and temporal patterns.

Users can explore fire observations through an interactive 3D globe, filter data by satellite sensor, examine historical fire activity, and view analytical summaries. The project also investigates cross-sensor matching using spatial and temporal proximity to understand when different satellites detect potentially related fire activity.

What are its benefits?

  • Makes large and complex satellite datasets easier to explore.
  • Provides a global view of fire observation patterns.
  • Helps compare observations from multiple satellite instruments.
  • Supports historical fire analysis and identification of potential hotspots.
  • Improves understanding of satellite detection differences and data limitations.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to make satellite-derived fire information more accessible and useful for researchers, environmental scientists, disaster management teams, and policymakers. FIRETRACE aims to support better wildfire monitoring, historical analysis, and evidence-based environmental decision-making. It is designed as an analytical support platform, not a replacement for official emergency alerts or ground-based verification.

What technologies did we use?

  • Programming languages: Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, SQL, HTML, and CSS.
  • Frontend: React, Vite, MapLibre GL, CesiumJS, and Recharts.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pandas, NumPy, GeoPandas, and Scikit-learn.
  • Data sources: NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire observation datasets.
  • Development tools: Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub, and npm.

How is the project creative?

FIRETRACE combines satellite observation analysis with an interactive 3D Earth visualization. Instead of presenting fire data only through static maps or spreadsheets, it allows users to explore observations geographically and historically. Its multi-satellite approach also investigates how different sensors observe fire activity and where their detections may overlap.

What factors did our team consider?

Our team considered data accuracy, satellite sensor differences, geographical coverage, observation timestamps, processing performance, scalability, usability, and scientific reliability. We also considered uncertainty: nearby detections are treated as potential matches rather than confirmed individual fires. The platform is designed to preserve data quality and communicate the limitations of satellite observations while remaining expandable for future analytical capabilities.
